We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),

To have $u(x)$ pass through the given data points and have the specified slopes at the end points, we require

$$
\alpha_ {i} + 4 \alpha_ {i - 1} + \alpha_ {i + 1} = 6 u _ {i}, \quad \alpha_ {1} - \alpha_ {- 1} = 2 d u _ {0} ^ {1}, \quad \alpha_ {N + 1} - \alpha_ {N - 1} = 2 d u _ {N} ^ {1}, \tag {16}
$$

where $u_{1}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to a}$ and $u_{N}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to b}$ . The shape of $B_{3}(x)$ is shown in Fig.(2a).

Since $B_{3}(x)$ is a piecewise polynomial and only its third derivative is discontinuous, it is simple to express $u(x)$ in terms of the functions $f_{3}(x)$ and evolve it. The change in the third derivative of $B_{3}(x)$ at $x = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$ is $\{1, -4, 6, -4, 1\}$ and therefore $C_{i}^{3} = \alpha_{i-2} - 4\alpha_{i-1} + 6\alpha_{i} - 4\alpha_{i+1} + \alpha_{i+2}$ . This should be modified at the ends because the interpolation extends (to a small but significant extent) outside the range $\{a, b\}$ . To avoid this error, the interpolation must be truncated at a and b by including its derivatives at the boundaries using $C_{0}^{1} = u_{0}^{1}$ , $C_{0}^{2} = \alpha_{-1} - 2\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1}$ , $C_{0}^{3} = \alpha_{-1} - 3\alpha_{0} + 3\alpha_{1} - \alpha_{2}$ and $C_{N}^{1} = -u_{N}^{1}$ , $C_{N}^{2} = -(\alpha_{N-1} - 2\alpha_{N} + \alpha_{N+1})$ , $C_{N}^{3} = -(\alpha_{N-2} - 3\alpha_{N-1} + 3\alpha_{N} - \alpha_{N+1})$ . Then the exact evolution of the truncated interpolation is (assuming $u(a) = u(b) = 0$ )

$$
\phi (x, t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N - 1} C _ {i} ^ {3} \chi_ {3} (x - x _ {i}) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {0} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - a) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {N} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - b). \tag {17}
$$

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

For example, with $N = 10$ , $u_{i} = \sin (\pi (i / 10)^{2})$ and $u_{N}^{1} = 0$ , $u_{N}^{1} = -\pi /5$ , then solving (16) for $\alpha_{i}$ leads to the B-spline interpolation in (15) and its evolution (17) shown in Fig.2(b). For the Gaussian asymptotic form, we take mass $M = \int_0^{10}\sin (\pi (x / 10)^2)\mathrm{d}x\approx$ 5.05, mass-median $\bar{x} = 6.49$ , and m-width $w = 1.38$ .

Figure 2: (a) The $B_{3}$ basis spline. (b) The evolution of a B-spline interpolation. The results (solid curves) are shown for a sequence of times, together with the Gaussian with the same initial median mass and m-width w. The unit of time is $w^{2}/\kappa$ .

# 3 Two-dimensional media

In one dimension, any initial piecewise polynomial can be evolved; but in a medium with two dimensions the previous method extends only to a set of polynomials each truncated to a rectangular region. For the efficiencies arising from any continuities across the boundaries to be realised, the boundaries for each polynomial must lie on a rectangular grid; but the spacings between the lines of the grid may vary.

# 3.1 Evolving a polynomial truncated by a rectangle

For an initial state $\phi (x,y,0)$ the evolution $\phi (x,y,t)$ can be found from the integral

$$
\phi (x, y, t) = \iint \chi (x - x ^ {\prime}, t) \chi (y - y ^ {\prime}, t) \phi (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}, 0) \mathrm{d} x ^ {\prime} \mathrm{d} y ^ {\prime}. \tag {18}
$$

We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

stage=initial_expandedrank=4query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:6:part:1point_id=2d561057-0c8d-592c-b79d-d33987fc6dbbdoc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=1chunk_index=6modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.3850score_vector=0.3536score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0156rerank_score=nullscore_composite=0.3850score_policy=weighted_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=nullexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=nullretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=nullretry_carry_forward_from_stage=nullretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=nullretry_carry_forward_score=nullagent_relevance_score=nullagent_relevance_label=nullagent_relevance_source=nullagent_relevance_cache_hit=nullagent_grade_cache_key=nullagent_relevance_keep=nullagent_relevance_drop=nullagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=nullagent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=null

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ .

To have $u(x)$ pass through the given data points and have the specified slopes at the end points, we require

$$
\alpha_ {i} + 4 \alpha_ {i - 1} + \alpha_ {i + 1} = 6 u _ {i}, \quad \alpha_ {1} - \alpha_ {- 1} = 2 d u _ {0} ^ {1}, \quad \alpha_ {N + 1} - \alpha_ {N - 1} = 2 d u _ {N} ^ {1}, \tag {16}
$$

where $u_{1}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to a}$ and $u_{N}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to b}$ . The shape of $B_{3}(x)$ is shown in Fig.(2a).

Since $B_{3}(x)$ is a piecewise polynomial and only its third derivative is discontinuous, it is simple to express $u(x)$ in terms of the functions $f_{3}(x)$ and evolve it. The change in the third derivative of $B_{3}(x)$ at $x = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$ is $\{1, -4, 6, -4, 1\}$ and therefore $C_{i}^{3} = \alpha_{i-2} - 4\alpha_{i-1} + 6\alpha_{i} - 4\alpha_{i+1} + \alpha_{i+2}$ . This should be modified at the ends because the interpolation extends (to a small but significant extent) outside the range $\{a, b\}$ . To avoid this error, the interpolation must be truncated at a and b by including its derivatives at the boundaries using $C_{0}^{1} = u_{0}^{1}$ , $C_{0}^{2} = \alpha_{-1} - 2\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1}$ , $C_{0}^{3} = \alpha_{-1} - 3\alpha_{0} + 3\alpha_{1} - \alpha_{2}$ and $C_{N}^{1} = -u_{N}^{1}$ , $C_{N}^{2} = -(\alpha_{N-1} - 2\alpha_{N} + \alpha_{N+1})$ , $C_{N}^{3} = -(\alpha_{N-2} - 3\alpha_{N-1} + 3\alpha_{N} - \alpha_{N+1})$ . Then the exact evolution of the truncated interpolation is (assuming $u(a) = u(b) = 0$ )

$$
\phi (x, t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N - 1} C _ {i} ^ {3} \chi_ {3} (x - x _ {i}) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {0} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - a) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {N} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - b). \tag {17}
$$

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

For example, with $N = 10$ , $u_{i} = \sin (\pi (i / 10)^{2})$ and $u_{N}^{1} = 0$ , $u_{N}^{1} = -\pi /5$ , then solving (16) for $\alpha_{i}$ leads to the B-spline interpolation in (15) and its evolution (17) shown in Fig.2(b). For the Gaussian asymptotic form, we take mass $M = \int_0^{10}\sin (\pi (x / 10)^2)\mathrm{d}x\approx$ 5.05, mass-median $\bar{x} = 6.49$ , and m-width $w = 1.38$ .

Figure 2: (a) The $B_{3}$ basis spline. (b) The evolution of a B-spline interpolation. The results (solid curves) are shown for a sequence of times, together with the Gaussian with the same initial median mass and m-width w. The unit of time is $w^{2}/\kappa$ .

# 3 Two-dimensional media

In one dimension, any initial piecewise polynomial can be evolved; but in a medium with two dimensions the previous method extends only to a set of polynomials each truncated to a rectangular region. For the efficiencies arising from any continuities across the boundaries to be realised, the boundaries for each polynomial must lie on a rectangular grid; but the spacings between the lines of the grid may vary.

# 3.1 Evolving a polynomial truncated by a rectangle

For an initial state $\phi (x,y,0)$ the evolution $\phi (x,y,t)$ can be found from the integral

$$
\phi (x, y, t) = \iint \chi (x - x ^ {\prime}, t) \chi (y - y ^ {\prime}, t) \phi (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}, 0) \mathrm{d} x ^ {\prime} \mathrm{d} y ^ {\prime}. \tag {18}
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

stage=rerankrank=2query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:6:part:1point_id=2d561057-0c8d-592c-b79d-d33987fc6dbbdoc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=1chunk_index=6modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.5037score_vector=0.3536score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0156rerank_score=0.7015score_composite=0.5037score_policy=weighted_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=nullexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=nullretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=nullretry_carry_forward_from_stage=nullretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=nullretry_carry_forward_score=nullagent_relevance_score=nullagent_relevance_label=nullagent_relevance_source=nullagent_relevance_cache_hit=nullagent_grade_cache_key=nullagent_relevance_keep=nullagent_relevance_drop=nullagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=nullagent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=null
, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

stage=rerankrank=4query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:8:part:0point_id=401a79fd-e0c8-51f8-b15f-25f86570aefadoc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=2chunk_index=8modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.3894score_vector=0.2938score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0143rerank_score=0.5831score_composite=0.3894score_policy=weighted_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=nullexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=nullretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=nullretry_carry_forward_from_stage=nullretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=nullretry_carry_forward_score=nullagent_relevance_score=nullagent_relevance_label=nullagent_relevance_source=nullagent_relevance_cache_hit=nullagent_grade_cache_key=nullagent_relevance_keep=nullagent_relevance_drop=nullagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=nullagent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=null
\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

stage=rerankrank=6query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:7:part:0point_id=d50023d7-2af7-5c75-b22a-2e0660d6d7a7doc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=1chunk_index=7modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.4824score_vector=0.3734score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0164rerank_score=0.5597score_composite=0.4824score_policy=weighted_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=nullexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=nullretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=nullretry_carry_forward_from_stage=nullretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=nullretry_carry_forward_score=nullagent_relevance_score=nullagent_relevance_label=nullagent_relevance_source=nullagent_relevance_cache_hit=nullagent_grade_cache_key=nullagent_relevance_keep=nullagent_relevance_drop=nullagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=nullagent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=null
We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

  "text": "We denote\n\n$$\n\\Phi_ {0} = \\frac {4 \\pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \\tag {1}\n$$\n\nwhere c is the speed of light. At $\\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \\rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\\boldsymbol{A}(\\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\\boldsymbol{B}(\\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\\boldsymbol{E}(\\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,\n\n$$\n\\boldsymbol {A} (\\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \\boldsymbol {\\nu} \\times \\boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \\boldsymbol {B} (\\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \\boldsymbol {\\nu} B (r, t),\n$$\n\n$$\n\\boldsymbol {E} (\\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \\boldsymbol {\\nu} \\times \\boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),\n$$\n\n$$\nA (r, t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \\sin (\\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \\cos (\\omega t) ],\n$$\n\n$$\nB (r, t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \\sin (\\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \\cos (\\omega t) ],\n$$\n\n$$\nE (r, t) = - \\Phi_ {0} \\frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \\cos (\\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \\sin (\\omega t) ], \\tag {2}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\pmb{\\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\\pmb{n} = \\pmb{r}/r$ , $\\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \\omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.\n\nFor $kr \\ll 1$ we have\n\n$$\nA (r, t) = \\frac {\\Phi_ {0}}{2 \\pi r} \\cos (\\omega t),\n$$\n\n$$\nB (r, t) = k ^ {2} \\frac {\\Phi_ {0}}{2 \\pi} \\ln (k r) \\cos (\\omega t),\n$$\n\n$$\nE (r, t) = k \\frac {\\Phi_ {0}}{2 \\pi r} \\sin (\\omega t). \\tag {3}\n$$\n\nFor $kr \\gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are\n\n$$\nA (r, t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\sqrt {\\frac {k}{8 \\pi r}} \\cos (\\omega t - k r + \\pi / 4),\n$$",

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),

Formula (display): d \sigma (\theta , \tau) = \frac {\hbar}{2 \pi P} \left| \int_ {- \infty} ^ {+ \infty} d y e ^ {- i s y} \left[ 1 - e ^ {- i \Xi (y, \tau)} \right] \right| ^ {2} \frac {d \theta}{\theta^ {2}},

\Xi (y, \tau) = \frac {\zeta y Q}{2} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \frac {d z}{r} \left[ J _ {1} (\zeta r) \sin (\phi) - N _ {1} (\zeta r) \cos (\phi) \right],

\zeta = \frac {k}{| q |} = \frac {\hbar k}{P \theta}, Q = \frac {e \Phi_ {0}}{2 c \hbar}, \phi = \tau + \frac {c}{v} \zeta z,

r = \sqrt {y ^ {2} + z ^ {2}}, \quad s = \operatorname{sgn} q. \tag {13}

To have $u(x)$ pass through the given data points and have the specified slopes at the end points, we require

$$
\alpha_ {i} + 4 \alpha_ {i - 1} + \alpha_ {i + 1} = 6 u _ {i}, \quad \alpha_ {1} - \alpha_ {- 1} = 2 d u _ {0} ^ {1}, \quad \alpha_ {N + 1} - \alpha_ {N - 1} = 2 d u _ {N} ^ {1}, \tag {16}
$$

where $u_{1}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to a}$ and $u_{N}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to b}$ . The shape of $B_{3}(x)$ is shown in Fig.(2a).

Since $B_{3}(x)$ is a piecewise polynomial and only its third derivative is discontinuous, it is simple to express $u(x)$ in terms of the functions $f_{3}(x)$ and evolve it. The change in the third derivative of $B_{3}(x)$ at $x = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$ is $\{1, -4, 6, -4, 1\}$ and therefore $C_{i}^{3} = \alpha_{i-2} - 4\alpha_{i-1} + 6\alpha_{i} - 4\alpha_{i+1} + \alpha_{i+2}$ . This should be modified at the ends because the interpolation extends (to a small but significant extent) outside the range $\{a, b\}$ . To avoid this error, the interpolation must be truncated at a and b by including its derivatives at the boundaries using $C_{0}^{1} = u_{0}^{1}$ , $C_{0}^{2} = \alpha_{-1} - 2\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1}$ , $C_{0}^{3} = \alpha_{-1} - 3\alpha_{0} + 3\alpha_{1} - \alpha_{2}$ and $C_{N}^{1} = -u_{N}^{1}$ , $C_{N}^{2} = -(\alpha_{N-1} - 2\alpha_{N} + \alpha_{N+1})$ , $C_{N}^{3} = -(\alpha_{N-2} - 3\alpha_{N-1} + 3\alpha_{N} - \alpha_{N+1})$ . Then the exact evolution of the truncated interpolation is (assuming $u(a) = u(b) = 0$ )

$$
\phi (x, t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N - 1} C _ {i} ^ {3} \chi_ {3} (x - x _ {i}) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {0} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - a) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {N} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - b). \tag {17}
$$

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

For example, with $N = 10$ , $u_{i} = \sin (\pi (i / 10)^{2})$ and $u_{N}^{1} = 0$ , $u_{N}^{1} = -\pi /5$ , then solving (16) for $\alpha_{i}$ leads to the B-spline interpolation in (15) and its evolution (17) shown in Fig.2(b). For the Gaussian asymptotic form, we take mass $M = \int_0^{10}\sin (\pi (x / 10)^2)\mathrm{d}x\approx$ 5.05, mass-median $\bar{x} = 6.49$ , and m-width $w = 1.38$ .

Figure 2: (a) The $B_{3}$ basis spline. (b) The evolution of a B-spline interpolation. The results (solid curves) are shown for a sequence of times, together with the Gaussian with the same initial median mass and m-width w. The unit of time is $w^{2}/\kappa$ .

# 3 Two-dimensional media

In one dimension, any initial piecewise polynomial can be evolved; but in a medium with two dimensions the previous method extends only to a set of polynomials each truncated to a rectangular region. For the efficiencies arising from any continuities across the boundaries to be realised, the boundaries for each polynomial must lie on a rectangular grid; but the spacings between the lines of the grid may vary.

# 3.1 Evolving a polynomial truncated by a rectangle

For an initial state $\phi (x,y,0)$ the evolution $\phi (x,y,t)$ can be found from the integral

$$
\phi (x, y, t) = \iint \chi (x - x ^ {\prime}, t) \chi (y - y ^ {\prime}, t) \phi (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}, 0) \mathrm{d} x ^ {\prime} \mathrm{d} y ^ {\prime}. \tag {18}
$$

We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),

  "text": "t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\sqrt {\\frac {k}{8 \\pi r}} \\cos (\\omega t - k r + \\pi / 4),\n$$\n\n$$\nB (r, t) = - \\Phi_ {0} k \\sqrt {\\frac {k}{8 \\pi r}} \\sin (\\omega t - k r + \\pi / 4),\n$$\n\n$$\nE (r, t) = k \\Phi_ {0} \\sqrt {\\frac {k}{8 \\pi r}} \\sin (\\omega t - k r + \\pi / 4). \\tag {4}\n$$\n\nThese asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.\n\nWe consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \\ll 1$ .",

To have $u(x)$ pass through the given data points and have the specified slopes at the end points, we require

$$
\alpha_ {i} + 4 \alpha_ {i - 1} + \alpha_ {i + 1} = 6 u _ {i}, \quad \alpha_ {1} - \alpha_ {- 1} = 2 d u _ {0} ^ {1}, \quad \alpha_ {N + 1} - \alpha_ {N - 1} = 2 d u _ {N} ^ {1}, \tag {16}
$$

where $u_{1}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to a}$ and $u_{N}^{1}=\partial_{x}u(x)_{x\to b}$ . The shape of $B_{3}(x)$ is shown in Fig.(2a).

Since $B_{3}(x)$ is a piecewise polynomial and only its third derivative is discontinuous, it is simple to express $u(x)$ in terms of the functions $f_{3}(x)$ and evolve it. The change in the third derivative of $B_{3}(x)$ at $x = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$ is $\{1, -4, 6, -4, 1\}$ and therefore $C_{i}^{3} = \alpha_{i-2} - 4\alpha_{i-1} + 6\alpha_{i} - 4\alpha_{i+1} + \alpha_{i+2}$ . This should be modified at the ends because the interpolation extends (to a small but significant extent) outside the range $\{a, b\}$ . To avoid this error, the interpolation must be truncated at a and b by including its derivatives at the boundaries using $C_{0}^{1} = u_{0}^{1}$ , $C_{0}^{2} = \alpha_{-1} - 2\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1}$ , $C_{0}^{3} = \alpha_{-1} - 3\alpha_{0} + 3\alpha_{1} - \alpha_{2}$ and $C_{N}^{1} = -u_{N}^{1}$ , $C_{N}^{2} = -(\alpha_{N-1} - 2\alpha_{N} + \alpha_{N+1})$ , $C_{N}^{3} = -(\alpha_{N-2} - 3\alpha_{N-1} + 3\alpha_{N} - \alpha_{N+1})$ . Then the exact evolution of the truncated interpolation is (assuming $u(a) = u(b) = 0$ )

$$
\phi (x, t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N - 1} C _ {i} ^ {3} \chi_ {3} (x - x _ {i}) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {0} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - a) + \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {3} C _ {N} ^ {p} \chi_ {p} (x - b). \tag {17}
$$

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

For example, with $N = 10$ , $u_{i} = \sin (\pi (i / 10)^{2})$ and $u_{N}^{1} = 0$ , $u_{N}^{1} = -\pi /5$ , then solving (16) for $\alpha_{i}$ leads to the B-spline interpolation in (15) and its evolution (17) shown in Fig.2(b). For the Gaussian asymptotic form, we take mass $M = \int_0^{10}\sin (\pi (x / 10)^2)\mathrm{d}x\approx$ 5.05, mass-median $\bar{x} = 6.49$ , and m-width $w = 1.38$ .

Figure 2: (a) The $B_{3}$ basis spline. (b) The evolution of a B-spline interpolation. The results (solid curves) are shown for a sequence of times, together with the Gaussian with the same initial median mass and m-width w. The unit of time is $w^{2}/\kappa$ .

# 3 Two-dimensional media

In one dimension, any initial piecewise polynomial can be evolved; but in a medium with two dimensions the previous method extends only to a set of polynomials each truncated to a rectangular region. For the efficiencies arising from any continuities across the boundaries to be realised, the boundaries for each polynomial must lie on a rectangular grid; but the spacings between the lines of the grid may vary.

# 3.1 Evolving a polynomial truncated by a rectangle

For an initial state $\phi (x,y,0)$ the evolution $\phi (x,y,t)$ can be found from the integral

$$
\phi (x, y, t) = \iint \chi (x - x ^ {\prime}, t) \chi (y - y ^ {\prime}, t) \phi (x ^ {\prime}, y ^ {\prime}, 0) \mathrm{d} x ^ {\prime} \mathrm{d} y ^ {\prime}. \tag {18}
$$

# 文章：什么时候该用 $< \mathrm{a}>$ ？

当你的意图是“导航到某个资源”时，用链接很合适；如果是触发动作（比如打开弹窗），通常更该用<button>。

小提示：你也可以用链接跳到页面内的某个位置，比如跳到联系信息。

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<summary>line</summary>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

stage=agent_chunk_gradingrank=6query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:7:part:0point_id=d50023d7-2af7-5c75-b22a-2e0660d6d7a7doc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=1chunk_index=7modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.5800score_vector=0.3734score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0164rerank_score=0.5600score_composite=0.5800score_policy=weighted_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=retry_carry_forwardexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=Trueretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=Trueretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=Trueretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=0.4360retry_carry_forward_from_stage=agent_chunk_gradingretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=6retry_carry_forward_score=0.6024agent_relevance_score=0.9700agent_relevance_label=strongagent_relevance_source=cacheagent_relevance_cache_hit=Trueagent_grade_cache_key=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:7:part:0agent_relevance_keep=Trueagent_relevance_drop=Falseagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=0.0agent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=Contains formula with n and explicitly ties it to the solenoid, supporting that n denotes turns per unit length.
We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

Figure 1. Dependence of $\Sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{s}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (top plot) and $\Sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)=\sigma_{0}^{-1}d\sigma_{a}(\vartheta,\tau)/d\vartheta$ (bottom plot) on $\vartheta$ for f=2 (solid curve), f=3 (dashed curve) and f=4 (dotted curve), $f=Q\cos\tau$ .   
![](images/11b6cb6bb6e89aace75756a2cc1fe8d9b6b31902b1ce08266c810ecedfead7f2.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

Figure 2. Dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ for Q=1 (solid curve), Q=2 (dashed curve) and Q=3 (dotted curve).

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

The total cross section averaged over time may also be of interest,

$$
\overline {{\sigma}} (Q) = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \sigma (\tau) \frac {d \tau}{2 \pi} = \pi \sigma_ {0} \int_ {0} ^ {1} [ 1 - J _ {0} (Q y) ] \frac {d y}{y}. \tag {21}
$$

The dependence of $\overline{\Sigma}_{tot}(Q) = \overline{\sigma}(Q) / \sigma_0$ on $Q$ is shown in

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

stage=evidence_gaterank=4query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:8:part:0point_id=401a79fd-e0c8-51f8-b15f-25f86570aefadoc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=2chunk_index=8modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.1893score_vector=0.2938score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0143rerank_score=0.5828score_composite=0.1893score_policy=agent_chunk_label_delta_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=nullexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=nullretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=nullretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=nullretry_carry_forward_from_stage=nullretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=nullretry_carry_forward_score=nullagent_relevance_score=0.0200agent_relevance_label=irrelevantagent_relevance_source=cacheagent_relevance_cache_hit=Trueagent_grade_cache_key=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:8:part:0agent_relevance_keep=Trueagent_relevance_drop=Falseagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=-0.2agent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=Discusses Pauli equation and periodicity, not the asked figure curve style or symbol n.
\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

stage=evidence_gaterank=6query_text=Based on the crops, which curve style represents Q = 3, and what symbol denotes the solenoid's number of turns per unit length?node_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:7:part:0point_id=d50023d7-2af7-5c75-b22a-2e0660d6d7a7doc_id=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4source=data\demo_docs\2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effect.pdftitle=2412.16030_Non-stationary_Aharonov-Bohm_effectpage=1chunk_index=7modality=textchannel=vectorvector_name=textparser_name=minerusource_parser=mineruscore=0.5800score_vector=0.3734score_bm25=nullscore_rrf=0.0164rerank_score=0.5600score_composite=0.5800score_policy=weighted_v1threshold_passed=Trueexpanded_from=nullexpansion_relation=nullcandidate_pool=retry_carry_forwardexpansion_mode=nullexpansion_allowed_by=nullseed_rank=nullseed_threshold=nullrelation_priority=nullreplaced_relation=nullretry_carry_forward=Trueretry_carry_forward_added=nullretry_carry_forward_matched=Trueretry_carry_forward_replaced_current=Trueretry_carry_forward_replaced_current_score=0.4360retry_carry_forward_from_stage=agent_chunk_gradingretry_carry_forward_previous_rank=6retry_carry_forward_score=0.6024agent_relevance_score=0.9700agent_relevance_label=strongagent_relevance_source=cacheagent_relevance_cache_hit=Trueagent_grade_cache_key=bad4486a9b70f8e94b4a5b409d3ffdb4:text:7:part:0agent_relevance_keep=Trueagent_relevance_drop=Falseagent_relevance_drop_cached=nullagent_label_score_delta=0.0agent_related_modality_delta=nullagent_related_context_text_delta=nullagent_related_context_node_id=nullagent_related_context_present=nullagent_related_context_added=nullagent_related_context_fixed_score=nullagent_relevance_reasoning=Contains formula with n and explicitly ties it to the solenoid, supporting that n denotes turns per unit length.
We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

The total cross section increases with $Q$ and is well approximated at $Q \gg 1$ by the formula

$$
\sigma (\tau) \approx \pi \sigma_ {0} \ln (1 + 2 Q | \cos \tau |).
$$

$$

We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ . Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,

$$
\boldsymbol {A} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \boldsymbol {B} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \boldsymbol {\nu} B (r, t),
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {E} (\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \boldsymbol {\nu} \times \boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),
$$

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
B (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \sin (\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \cos (\omega t) ],
$$

$$
E (r, t) = - \Phi_ {0} \frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \cos (\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \sin (\omega t) ], \tag {2}
$$

where $\pmb{\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\pmb{n} = \pmb{r}/r$ , $\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.

For $kr \ll 1$ we have

$$
A (r, t) = \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
B (r, t) = k ^ {2} \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi} \ln (k r) \cos (\omega t),
$$

$$
E (r, t) = k \frac {\Phi_ {0}}{2 \pi r} \sin (\omega t). \tag {3}
$$

For $kr \gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are

$$
A (r, t) = \Phi_ {0} \sqrt {\frac {k}{8 \pi r}} \cos (\omega t - k r + \pi / 4),
$$

Solving Maxwell equation, we find the vector-potential $\\boldsymbol{A}(\\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ , the magnetic field $\\boldsymbol{B}(\\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ and the electric field $\\boldsymbol{E}(\\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ outside the solenoid,\n\n$$\n\\boldsymbol {A} (\\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \\boldsymbol {\\nu} \\times \\boldsymbol {n} ] A (r, t), \\boldsymbol {B} (\\boldsymbol {r}, t) = \\boldsymbol {\\nu} B (r, t),\n$$\n\n$$\n\\boldsymbol {E} (\\boldsymbol {r}, t) = [ \\boldsymbol {\\nu} \\times \\boldsymbol {n} ] E (r, t),\n$$\n\n$$\nA (r, t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\frac {k}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \\sin (\\omega t) - N _ {1} (k r) \\cos (\\omega t) ],\n$$\n\n$$\nB (r, t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ - J _ {0} (k r) \\sin (\\omega t) + N _ {0} (k r) \\cos (\\omega t) ],\n$$\n\n$$\nE (r, t) = - \\Phi_ {0} \\frac {k ^ {2}}{4} [ J _ {1} (k r) \\cos (\\omega t) + N _ {1} (k r) \\sin (\\omega t) ], \\tag {2}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\pmb{\\nu}$ is a unit vector directed along the z-axis and parallel to the solenoid axis, $\\pmb{n} = \\pmb{r}/r$ , $\\pmb{r} = (x, y, 0)$ , $r = \\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$ , $k = \\omega/c$ , $J_{l}(x)$ is the Bessel function, $N_{l}(x)$ is the Neumann function.\n\nFor $kr \\ll 1$ we have\n\n$$\nA (r, t) = \\frac {\\Phi_ {0}}{2 \\pi r} \\cos (\\omega t),\n$$\n\n$$\nB (r, t) = k ^ {2} \\frac {\\Phi_ {0}}{2 \\pi} \\ln (k r) \\cos (\\omega t),\n$$\n\n$$\nE (r, t) = k \\frac {\\Phi_ {0}}{2 \\pi r} \\sin (\\omega t). \\tag {3}\n$$\n\nFor $kr \\gg 1$ the asymptotics of fields are\n\n$$\nA (r, t) = \\Phi_ {0} \\sqrt {\\frac {k}{8 \\pi r}} \\cos (\\omega t - k r + \\pi / 4),\n$$",

, the electric and magnetic fields outside the solenoid will be equal to zero.

However, if the current in the solenoid is alternating, the electromagnetic fields will be non-zero in the accessible to the electron motion region. In this case, the topology of the space accessible to the electron motion is the same as that in the stationary case, so that the influence of alternating magnetic field flux inside the solenoid on the electron motion outside the solenoid (the non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect) will be somewhat similar to the stationary effect, but will also have some differences. The non-stationary Aharonov-Bohm effect has been discussed in many papers with contradictory results (see, for example, $[3–8]$ ). However, none of these papers calculated such experimentally important quantities as the differential and total scattering cross sections. Our work is devoted to the study of these quantities.

# II. EIKONAL APPROXIMATION AND THE CROSS SECTION OF NON-STATIONARY AHARONOV-BOHM EFFECT

Let us consider an infinitely long solenoid with radius $a$ and the number $n$ of turns per unit length, through which a current $I(t) = I_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is passed. We denote

$$
\Phi_ {0} = \frac {4 \pi^ {2} a ^ {2}}{c} n I _ {0}, \tag {1}
$$

where c is the speed of light. At $\omega = 0$ this quantity coincides with the magnetic field flux through the solenoid. We are interested in the limit $a \rightarrow 0$ at a fixed value of $\Phi_{0}$ .

\tag {4}
$$

These asymptotics correspond to the radiation field of a solenoid.

We consider a non-relativistic problem, so that we assume that the electron velocity v satisfies the condition $v/c \ll 1$ . The Pauli equation for the wave function $\psi(\boldsymbol{r}, t)$ of an electron in the field of a solenoid reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\pmb {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\pmb {p} - \frac {e}{c} [ \pmb {\nu} \times \pmb {n} ] A (r, t)\right) ^ {2} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {5} \\ \end{array}
$$

where M, e and $\mu$ are the mass, charge and magnetic moment of electron, $\lambda = \pm1$ corresponds to the projection $\pm1/2$ of spin onto the z axis. Since $A(r,t)$ and $B(r,t)$ are periodic functions in t with the period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ , the wave function satisfies the periodicity condition [9, 10],

$$
\psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t + T) = e ^ {i \alpha T} \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t). \tag {6}
$$

Let us rewrite the Pauli equation in the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} i \hbar \frac {\partial \psi (\boldsymbol {r} , t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac {\boldsymbol {p} ^ {2}}{2 M} - \frac {e \hbar A (r , t)}{M c r} l _ {z} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {e ^ {2} A ^ {2} (r , t)}{2 M c ^ {2}} - \lambda \mu B (r, t) \right] \psi (\boldsymbol {r}, t), \tag {7} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $l_{z} = (xp_{y} - yp_{x})/\hbar$ is the projection operator of orbital momentum onto the z axis. Let the momentum of incident electron be P. From the experimental point of view, the momenta $P \gg \hbar k$ and small scattering angles $\theta \ll 1$ are of interest, while the relationship between $q = P\theta/\hbar$ and k can be arbitrary.

Naturally, there is no asymmetry in $\sigma(\tau)$ . The dependence of $\Sigma_{tot}(\tau)=\sigma(\tau)/\sigma_{0}$ on $\tau$ is shown in Fig.2 for several values of Q.

![](images/1b7ffdcf3a86d09e9a2953e40a0196a8b8d4ea16c8d7eab29b8b93214871675a.jpg)

<details>
<summary>line</summary>


</details>

![](images/6702d0432117e9c2c1065da445998cb9174570bd2d519804540866ab6cf10e5a.jpg)

<details>
